_comment: Each entry pairs a bug that reached production with the test that must catch it.
verify-guards.sh applies the mutation, runs only the named test file, and
requires it to FAIL. A guard that still passes under mutation is not a guard.
'find' must match exactly once. If it stops matching, the guarded code has
changed and the job fails as STALE -- distinctly from a guard failure, because
the two need different responses: stale means re-verify the guard still covers
the bug; failure means the guard has stopped working.

mutations.bug: ACP checkout returned 404 on every route; the /acp prefix was not stripped before dispatch (#62)
Eight routes unreachable in production, including all health/metrics and the /v1/orgs family (#69)
POST /v1/analyze raised for every authenticated caller; the ETS table was created in Plug init/1, which runs at compile time (#91)
mutations.find:
# Belt and braces: rate limiting must never be the reason an analysis fails.
    init_table()

mutations.bug: Every completed Pro checkout ended on a 500; get_session/2 was called without fetching the session (#90)
Unauthenticated signup issued an admin-scoped key for an existing org when the name matched (#89)
ACP endpoints had no rate limiting; an unauthenticated caller could create unbounded sessions, orgs and API keys

Anticipated, not yet shipped: a replayed Stripe webhook or resubmitted x402 payment proof double-credits an org. The defence is the unique index on external_ref, surfaced through the changeset constraint -- without it a duplicate raises Ecto.ConstraintError instead of returning {:error, :duplicate}, which callers will not be expecting.

A failed scan left the BEAM's working directory inside a checkout that was then deleted. cwd is node-global, so every later relative path failed with 'could not get current working directory'. Surfaced as an order-dependent cascade in CI that the test retry loop had been hiding (#108).
mutations.find:
try do
      File.cd!(path)
      fun.()
    after
      File.cd!(cwd)
    end

mutations.bug: GET /url= hung forever in production. find_binary_files shelled out to `grep -rIL .` with no file operand: GNU grep searches the working directory, BusyBox grep -- what the Alpine runtime image provides -- reads stdin, and System.cmd holds the child's stdin open forever. No assertion about grep's behaviour can catch this on a machine with GNU grep, so the guard is the absence of the external process: the test runs with PATH emptied.
mutations.replace: |> Stream.filter(fn f -> match?({_, 0}, System.cmd("grep", ["-qI", ".", f])) end)

mutations.bug: A wrong STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET failed identically to an unset one and to a scanner POSTing junk -- all three returned 400 with no way to tell them apart. The secret sat set-but-wrong with webhooks silently 400ing and nothing surfaced it. Collapsing 'unconfigured' back into 'invalid' makes the monitor report a rotation problem when the real fault is a missing secret.

The usage row and its ledger debit are one transaction because they describe the same event: a committed usage row with no debit is an analysis delivered and never accounted for, findable only by reconciliation after the fact. Letting a failed debit fall through instead of rolling back recreates that gap on every failure.
Anticipated: dropping the ledger debit from the usage path leaves analyses consumed with no internal record of what they cost, which is the state ADR-002 exists to end.

A wallet address is public, so provisioning that returns an existing org for a presented address hands an attacker a credential for someone else's funded org -- #89's bug in a new costume. provision/2 must never return an existing org; only the caller, having proved control, may decide that.

A wallet costs nothing to create, so any per-wallet free allowance is a per-attacker free allowance. Giving wallet orgs the default free-tier limit reopens the farming vector ADR-002 closes by granting none.

A wallet org's only gate is its credit balance, checked before the analysis runs. Falling through to the tier check would serve a zero-balance agent for free, and ADR-002 allows balances to go negative precisely because refusal has to happen before the work.
mutations.find:
%Org{wallet_address: wallet} = org when is_binary(wallet) and wallet != "" ->
        check_credit_balance(org)

mutations.bug: The boundary for 'pre-ledger' usage must fail towards reporting. Excusing every row when no boundary can be derived means an un-debited system reports clean having reconciled nothing -- the failure this module exists to catch, written into it. Separately, the boundary is the first debit and not the migration timestamp: the credit_entries table existed sixteen hours before anything wrote to it in production, and seven usage rows recorded in between were reported as drift.
A balance is money. /v1/credits derives org_id from the authenticated API key and nothing else; taking it from a query parameter would let any key read any org's ledger.

The Stripe meter call happens outside the usage transaction and its result was discarded -- so a failed call meant usage consumed, ledger debited, customer never billed, with nothing written down. Under-billing that errs against us, and invisible. Dropping the failure record restores that blind spot.

No /v1/cache route enforced any scope and LowendinsightGet.Auth did not either -- it authenticated and stopped. Any API key that could call the API could export every cached report, or import over them and change the answers everyone else received.
mutations.find: if conn.assigns[:auth_method] == :jwt or has_scope?(conn, required) do

mutations.bug: The landing page's Try it form lacked the analyze-button and invalid-url elements endpoints.js reaches by id. disable_button did null.classList.add, and since validate_and_submit calls preventDefault first, the throw left the form never submitting -- clicking Analyze did nothing, with the reason visible only in the browser console. Server-side the template rendered, the asset returned 200, and the route worked when called directly.

Browsers request /favicon.ico from the root whether or not a link tag points at it. Plug.Static is mounted at /images, /js and /css, none of which cover the root, so without a dedicated mount the request 404s on every page load and no page-scanning check can notice -- nothing links to it.

The dark media query is guarded with :not([data-theme="light"]) so an explicit light choice survives a dark system setting. Without the guard the toggle only works in one direction: a user on a dark system who picks light gets dark back, with no way to say otherwise.

The signup, login and dashboard pages render through a layout in the other app's directory, so a coverage check globbing this app's templates never saw it and they shipped without favicon links. The check now renders the real routes, so removing the links fails rather than going unnoticed.
mutations.find:
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
  <link rel="icon" type="image/png" sizes="32x32" href="/images/favicon-32.png">
  <link rel="icon" type="image/png" sizes="16x16" href="/images/favicon-16.png">
  <link rel="apple-touch-icon" sizes="180x180" href="/images/apple-touch-icon.png">

mutations.bug: Every payment rail, on either side, credits the ledger through one function so there is a single idempotency boundary. Dropping the external_ref makes a replayed webhook or resubmitted payment proof credit twice -- duplicate settlement under concurrency being both a documented x402 attack class and this codebase's recurring failure.

external_ref is globally unique, so writing a rail's raw reference into it means two rails that ever mint the same string collapse into one another. Because {:error, :duplicate} is documented as an expected retry outcome, a caller following that contract treats a real second payment as an already-handled replay: money taken, no credits granted, and nothing in an append-only ledger to find it by.

Rails commonly identify a refund by the payment it reverses. Sharing the purchase's namespace means the reversal collides with its own original on external_ref and is refused as a duplicate -- the money goes back and nothing in the ledger records it.

Rails declare which cadences they support and what they cost to collect through. Unchecked, a rail that declares none can never sell anything, and one declaring both :streaming and a minimum purchase has a contradiction -- streaming settles per interaction, so there is no purchase to apply a minimum to. Either is discovered at the first payment, which means discovered from a customer.

Cross-resource substitution is the documented x402 flaw, and its root cause is signatures that carry no context about what they pay for. MPP's credential echoes the challenge so the server can check it. Comparing only the id lets a client echo the right id while restating the price, which is a valid payment for something cheaper.
mutations.find:
echoed["id"] == issued.id and
      echoed["realm"] == issued.realm and
      echoed["method"] == issued.method and
      echoed["intent"] == issued.intent and
      request_matches?(echoed["request"], issued.request)

mutations.bug: The credential echoes the challenge request and the comparison is byte-for-byte, so the encoding has to be JCS-canonical. Sorting pairs and then putting them back into a map does nothing -- the map re-orders them -- and Elixir maps of 32 keys or fewer iterate sorted anyway, so the mistake is invisible until a request has 33 keys. At that point the bytes stop matching what the payment network signed and a legitimate payment is refused.

A credential proves a payment happened; it does not prove who it was for. Crediting whoever presents one lets an intercepted credential top up the wrong org -- the payer's money, someone else's balance. The org is taken from the recorded challenge, never from the request.
mutations.find: {:ok, org_id, issued_key} <- credit_payer(record, rail, settlement) do
mutations.replace: {:ok, org_id, issued_key} <- credit_payer(%{record | org_id: Keyword.get(opts, :org_id, record.org_id)}, rail, settlement) do

mutations.bug: A PaymentIntent that is processing, requires_action or requires_payment_method is not money. Accepting anything but a settled status gives away the work for a payment that may still fail, and the ledger records credits nobody paid for.

An agent paying with MPP puts its credential in Authorization, per the Payment auth scheme. Without a clause for it the value falls off the end of authenticate/1 and a paying agent gets a 500 for presenting a valid credential -- the one request it most needs to succeed.

The settle path is unauthenticated by necessity and every attempt can reach Stripe, which makes it the half an attacker would use to grind through stolen tokens. Without a bucket it is an unbounded outbound-request amplifier pointed at our own payment processor.

A wallet agent has no API key, so without billing context from the settled payment the quota check sees no org and is skipped entirely. The paid request is then served for the wrong reason -- not because it paid, but because nothing was checked -- and an unpaid one would be served identically.

purge_expired/1 existing is not the same as it running. Unanswered challenges are normal -- an agent asking the price and leaving -- and each is a row, so without a supervised sweep the table grows for as long as the service runs.

validate_rails!/0 passes trivially on an empty list: it refuses bad names and contradictory cadences, and an empty list has neither. The rail shipped unconfigured, so the boot guarantee was nominal -- a misnamed or contradictory rail would have sailed through because there were no rails to check. A check that passes by examining nothing.
A live Stripe key boots anywhere. A laptop or staging deploy holding a live key charges real cards, and nothing says so until a statement does (#137).
Mode reported from something other than the key prefix: restricted live keys (rk_live_) read as test, so /readyz and the canary report sandbox while real money moves (#137).
A publishable key or webhook secret in STRIPE_SECRET_KEY reads as 'billing off' rather than a mistake, boots, and fails at the first customer (#137).
An API key pasted into STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET boots, and every webhook delivery then fails verification silently -- the pre-#62 failure (#137).
Mode validation exists but is not called at boot, so every refusal it makes is unreachable in a running system (#137).
A price from the other mode (404, 'No such price') is classified as a transient outage: the canary lets it through and the half-flip ships (#137).
Production with no Stripe key or no price IDs reports ok: the check passes by examining nothing (#137).
The object check runs but is not registered with readiness, so a mismatch is logged and never reaches /readyz or monitoring (#137).
The serving mode is not exposed on /readyz, so the canary cannot assert it and a human cannot see it (#137).

ObjectCheck exists and is registered with readiness but never started: status/0 reads not_running forever, so readiness is degraded for a reason that says nothing about Stripe, and the price check never runs (#137).

The Shared Payment Token is sent as payment_method. Stripe answers 'No such PaymentMethod' and every real card payment over MPP fails; the rail tests mocked this boundary and asserted the wrong call (#143).
No Idempotency-Key on the SPT charge. An SPT is single-use, so an agent retrying after a timeout gets a second intent refused as 'deactivated' -- turned away after paying (observed in sandbox, #143).
requires_capture accepted as settled. That is an authorisation, funds held not taken; ADR-002 grants credits against settled money only (#143).
The challenge does not name the Stripe profile, so no agent wallet can mint a token scoped to us and the 402 is unpayable (#143).
A challenge is issued with no Stripe profile configured: it looks payable and fails at the wallet (#143).
A sandbox profile boots beside a live key: challenges name a profile no live wallet can pay (#143, extends #137).
A transfer is accepted without the challenge's memo. Hashes are public: anyone watching the chain can present another agent's payment to us as their own and take its credits. (#144)
A transfer to any address is accepted as payment to us. (#144)
A log from any contract is accepted, so a worthless look-alike token pays for credits. (#144)
Any four-topic event from the token is read as a transfer with memo. (#144)
A reverted transaction's logs are read as a payment that happened. (#144)
Stripe is asked, and credits granted, without the receipt binding the transfer to the challenge -- Stripe verifies the money but not whose it is. (#144)
An overpayment passes the chain check; Stripe then declines it invalid_amount with the agent's money already sent. (#144)
mutations.find: {:ok, %{amount: amount} = transfer} when amount == expected.amount -> {:ok, transfer}

mutations.bug: A challenge names a deposit address Stripe has not confirmed for this key. A sandbox address beside a live key takes mainnet funds Stripe never credits. (#144)
A challenge issued on testnet is verified against mainnet after a mode switch, or the reverse. (#144)
Each retry creates a new verification intent; Stripe refuses a second intent for one transfer, so the agent that paid is refused on retry. (#144)
A verification intent still processing is treated as settled -- credits for money Stripe has not confirmed, which a fabricated hash never will. (#144)
A deposit address absent from the key's account reads as ok, so a sandbox address beside a live key is confirmed. (#144)
mutations.find: if String.downcase(address) in addresses, do: "ok", else: "mismatch"

mutations.bug: deposit_address_confirmed?/1 answers yes without Stripe having listed the address. (#144)
The 402 offers only the first available rail, so an agent holding stablecoin is shown a card challenge it cannot answer. (#144)
mutations.find: offered = for {rail, {:ok, challenge}} <- results, do: {rail, challenge}
mutations.replace: offered = Enum.take(for({rail, {:ok, challenge}} <- results, do: {rail, challenge}), 1)

mutations.bug: A request with no org and no operator token is served rather than asked to pay -- free analysis for anyone who omits the Authorization header. (#147)
The deployed endpoint's auth plug answers an Authorization: Payment credential with 401, so no paying retry ever reaches settlement -- production's state for two releases. (#147)
An agent with no credentials is told to authenticate with something it cannot have, instead of being asked to pay. (#147)
Every /v1 route accepts unauthenticated requests, not just the paid analysis routes. (#147)
mutations.replace: do: method != nil and path != nil

mutations.bug: A card challenge is offered to a caller with no org. A card token identifies no payer, so the payment could create no org -- money taken, nobody to credit. (#147)
The agent that paid is not given a key, so the credits it bought are stranded: its next request is asked to pay again. (#147)
Tokens moved by an approved spender (transferFrom) identify the holder as payer, so anyone with an allowance can pay as a wallet and be issued its org and a key. (#147)
POST /v1/analyze bills only an API key's org. An agent that pays on the request has no key, so it is served with its balance never debited. (#147)
The settle rate limit is charged before looking for a credential, capping all analysis from one IP at 10 a minute. (#147)
Lei.Auth does not mark an operator JWT, so the gate treats an operator's request as an anonymous caller and asks it to pay. (#147)
A wallet org's analysed repository URLs are recorded next to its org and key on the admin dashboard -- the link between a paying wallet and what it analysed that was decided against. (#149)
mutations.find: urls = if withheld, do: [], else: repo_urls

mutations.bug: The request log attributes /v1/analyze only through an API key, so a paying agent's first request is logged with no org -- and, unrecognised as a wallet org, with its URLs. (#149)
The analysis worker names the repositories it processes at info, where production logs sit beside ledger timestamps. (#149)
Each analysis process logs its repository URL at info. (#149)
A cache hit logs the repository URL at info. (#149)
The homepage quotes a price that is not the rate the ledger charges, so a rate change leaves agents told the old price.
A cache hit's half cent is shown as $0.01, doubling the stated price.
The homepage says stablecoin is available when the rail would issue no challenge -- telling agents to pay a way that will refuse them.
The homepage describes live USDC payments while the service runs on a test key, or test mode after go-live.
The homepage stops pointing agents at /llms.txt.
mutations.find: <link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="/llms.txt" title="LowEndInsight for agents">

mutations.bug: POST /v1/analyze/sbom runs the analysis without debiting it: every repository an SBOM names, free. (#152)
POST /v1/analyze/sbom admits any key without checking balance or quota, so a wallet org with no credits is served. (#152)
/v1/analyze bills from nothing the request knew in advance -- an async analysis of an uncached repository is recorded as zero and collected later for free. (#152)
A credit-funded org holding less than a request costs is admitted and run into debt: an SBOM of hundreds of uncached repositories on a balance of five credits. (#152)
mutations.find: {:ok, balance} when required > 0 and balance < required ->
mutations.replace: {:ok, balance} when false and balance < required ->

mutations.bug: The top-up asked for is the default block even when the request needs more, so an agent pays and is refused again. (#152)
POST /v1/analyze/sbom answers an agent with no credentials 401 rather than asking it to pay. (#152)
The Try It form runs fresh analyses for any caller without limit -- a free analysis path around the 402. (#152)
Cached reports count against the Try It allowance, so a person browsing already-analysed repositories is refused. (#152)
Cleanup purges on the default minute, erasing an hourly bucket's history every two minutes so its limit is never reached. (#152)
Every bucket counts over the default minute, so an hourly limit is really a per-minute one. (#152)
Languages are analysed concurrently, so clones pile up until the 512 MB machine runs out of memory and every analysis dies -- production's state for days. (#158)
mutations.replace:
|> Task.async_stream(fn language -> {language, refresh(language, opts)} end, max_concurrency: 8, timeout: :infinity)
      |> Enum.map(fn {:ok, result} -> result end)

mutations.bug: A language's page is pointed at a report that has not completed, replacing the last good one with a placeholder that renders empty. (#158)
Every run redoes every language, so a run killed partway starts over and never reaches the end. (#158)
The hourly job and the manual trigger analyse at the same time, doubling the clones in memory. (#158)
An analysis that raises crashes the whole run instead of failing one language. (#158)
Repositories over the size limit are sent for analysis. (#158)
The hourly trending job may start while the previous run is still cloning. (#158)
Trending report completion and age are not on /metrics, so monitoring cannot see the job failing. (#158)
Shortlog UTF-8 repair splits the whole history into one binary per codepoint: elixir-lang/elixir's analysis went from ~180 MB to 572 MB RSS, the allocation that OOM-killed production (#158).
mutations.find: if String.valid?(binary), do: binary, else: repair_utf8(binary, 0, 0, [])
mutations.replace: binary |> String.codepoints() |> Enum.map(fn x -> if String.valid?(x), do: x, else: Enum.join(for(<<c <- x>>, do: <<c::utf8>>)) end) |> Enum.join()

mutations.bug: Agentic detection reads every commit body in history into memory, though only commits mentioning a co-author can match (#158).
The trending lock lasts six hours, so an OOM kill mid-run keeps the job from running for the rest of the day. (#158)
The lock is not extended as languages complete, so a long run loses it partway and the next hourly run starts alongside. (#158)
The size limit admits repositories up to 1 GB, several times the machine's memory. (#158)
The GitHub Search fallback returns the most-starred repositories with a recent push -- the largest, longest-history projects -- rather than rising ones. (#158)
OSS Insight's stated 'ranking unavailable' answer is reported as a generic empty result, hiding why trending runs on the fallback. (#158)
The trending job stays switched off: the pages go stale and monitoring only warns (#158).
The run-in-progress metric never reports a run, so the monitor fails -- and emails -- every 15 minutes while a first run fills in reports (#158 follow-up).

Analysis reports embed the whole application env: the Stripe secret key, webhook secret, session secret and JWT secret were published in every report, cached report, trending page and cache export (security, 2026-09-14).
